newsitem.title: GERMANY: Half Germans fear euro will damage economy-poll.
newsitem.headline: Half Germans fear euro will damage economy-poll.

text.p: About half of Germans expect Europe's planned single currency, the euro, to negatively affect their savings and the economy, according to a survey published on Friday.

The survey, conducted by the Institute for Market, Opinion and Economic Research based in Illereichen, southern Germany, showed 51 percent of Germans polled feared European economic and monetary union (EMU) would cut buying power and living standards and devalue savings.
More than two-thirds of the 970 Germans polled said they were convinced the euro would be weaker than the mark, the survey said.
The poll was the latest in a number of recent surveys to suggest Germans are getting cold feet about currency union, a project on which Chancellor Helmut Kohl has staked his reputation.
The institute's survey showed nearly 40 percent of Germans thought the euro would damage, rather than boost, the economy.
Of those polled, 27 percent believed the single currency was important, 23 percent said it was not important and 11 percent said they did not understand what the euro was about.

Bonn argues the single currency is necessary to boost Europe's flagging economies and to make post-World War Two peace irreversible. It says the euro will produce more jobs and tackle record unemployment, currently at 11 percent.

Kohl dismissed doubts about the euro's launch at a news conference earlier on Friday. He said Germany was economically strong enough to qualify for EMU and would join the euro's launch on January 1, 1999.
